name: Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma
aliases: hyalinizing spindle cell tumour with giant rosettes

clinicalPearls: A deceptively bland-looking sarcoma that, despite its innocuous histology, has genuine metastatic potential, often after a long interval
Typically presents as a painless deep soft-tissue mass in the trunk, limbs or limb girdles of young to middle-aged adults
Histology shows alternating fibrous and myxoid zones with bland spindle cells arranged in whorls and characteristic arcades of small curvilinear vessels
The great majority carry a FUS-CREB3L2 gene fusion, with a smaller proportion showing FUS-CREB3L1 or EWSR1-CREB3L1
Strong and diffuse MUC4 immunohistochemical expression is a highly sensitive and specific diagnostic marker
The hyalinizing spindle cell tumour with giant rosettes is a morphological variant within the same entity, featuring collagen rosettes
Because the cells look benign, the diagnosis is easily missed unless MUC4 staining or molecular testing is applied
reference.pathophysiology: Low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma is a fibroblastic malignancy defined by a recurrent gene fusion, most often FUS-CREB3L2, which joins an RNA-binding protein gene to a transcription-factor gene and deregulates downstream transcriptional programmes. This single driver produces a tumour of monotonous, cytologically bland spindle cells set in alternating collagenous and myxoid matrix. The fusion upregulates expression of MUC4, providing a reliable diagnostic marker, and although proliferation is low the tumour retains the capacity for late local recurrence and distant metastasis, underscoring its fully malignant nature.
additionalDifferentials: Perineurioma and other benign nerve sheath tumours
Sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma (which shares MUC4 expression and fusions)
additionalInvestigations: MUC4 immunohistochemistry as the key diagnostic screen
FISH or molecular testing for FUS and CREB3L2/CREB3L1 rearrangements
Panel to exclude nerve sheath tumours and fibromatosis (S100, SOX10, beta-catenin)
MRI to define the deep soft-tissue mass and plan resection
Staging chest imaging given the risk of late pulmonary metastasis
Long-term imaging surveillance because recurrence and metastasis can occur years later
redFlags: Late local recurrence or distant metastasis, often to the lungs, sometimes after many years
Increasing size or deep fixation of a previously stable mass
Areas of increased cellularity or higher-grade transformation within the tumour
Incomplete excision margins predisposing to recurrence
reference.prognosis: Although low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma grows slowly and looks histologically bland, it can recur locally and metastasise, characteristically to the lungs and sometimes decades after initial treatment; complete wide excision offers the best chance of cure, and prolonged follow-up is essential because the risk of late relapse persists.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the bland cytology as a benign fibrous or nerve sheath lesion
Omitting MUC4 staining, which readily distinguishes it from benign mimics
Discontinuing surveillance too early and missing late metastasis
Confusing it with sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma, which overlaps molecularly and by MUC4
Underestimating malignant potential because of the low mitotic rate
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
